The work scope for year 2013 monitoring was developed in cooperation with AES Laurel Mountain, LLC (AESLM), the US Fish and Wildlife Service Elkins Field Office (USFWS), and West Virginia Department of Natural Resources (WVDNR). Initially, Stantec searched all 61 Project turbines at a 3 day interval. In early June, the USFWS agreed to reduce monitoring effort to the subset of 24 turbines monitored during previous years, and to allow AESLM staff to search the remaining 37 turbines on a weekly basis.
All Project turbines were operated according to a sliding scale curtailment system developed for the Project by AESLM and approved by the USFWS in coordination with WVDNR. This system was based on bat activity patterns documented from acoustic detector surveys in the rotor zone of 6 Project turbines in fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 and included fully feathered turbines during particular combinations of [REDACTED] and wind speed based on predicted amount of bat activity. Cut-in wind speeds were higher as [REDACTED], up to a maximum of 8.5 m/s, and lower as [REDACTED]. The system was in place from 1 April through 15 November 2013.
A total of 22 bat and 42 bird carcasses were documented during the 2013 monitoring period. No threatened or endangered bird or bat species or bats of the genus Myotis were found. Seventeen bat carcasses and 29 bird carcasses were found at the 24 turbines monitored from 1 April – 15 November 2013 (study turbines) and the remainder were found at 37 turbines searched by Stantec from 1 April – 7 June and by AESLM staff from 11 June – 11 November. Fatality estimates for the 2013 monitoring period, based on the results at the 24 study turbines and taking into account search interval, carcass persistence, searcher efficiency, and an area correction factor, were 1.4 (95% CI 0.7 – 2.2) bats and 3.4 (95% CI 2.0 5.0) birds per turbine. The bat fatality rate for the 7.5 month 2013 monitoring period was 94% lower than the estimate for fully operational turbines based on the combined fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 6.5 month monitoring period (23.4 bats/turbine) and is estimated to be approximately 96% lower when normalized for equivalent monitoring periods.

## **Executive Summary**

Stantec Consulting Services Inc. (Stantec) conducted standardized post-construction bird and bat monitoring at the Laurel Mountain Wind Energy Project (Project) from 1 April to 15 November 2013. The work scope for year 2013 monitoring was developed in cooperation with AES Laurel Mountain, LLC (AESLM), the US Fish and Wildlife Service Elkins Field Office (USFWS), and West Virginia Department of Natural Resources (WVDNR). Initially, Stantec searched all 61 Project turbines at a 3 day interval. In early June, the USFWS agreed to reduce monitoring effort to the subset of 24 turbines monitored during previous years, and to allow AESLM staff to search the remaining 37 turbines on a weekly basis.

All Project turbines were operated according to a sliding scale curtailment system developed for the Project by AESLM and approved by the USFWS in coordination with WVDNR. This system was based on bat activity patterns documented from acoustic detector surveys in the rotor zone of 6 Project turbines in fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 and included fully feathered turbines during particular combinations of(b) (4) and wind speed based on predicted amount of bat activity. Cut-in wind speeds were higher as(b) (4) , up to a maximum of 8.5 m/s, and lower as(b) (4) . The system was in place from 1 April through 15 November 2013.

A total of 22 bat and 42 bird carcasses were documented during the 2013 monitoring period. No threatened or endangered bird or bat species or bats of the genus _Myotis_ were found. Seventeen bat carcasses and 29 bird carcasses were found at the 24 turbines monitored from 1 April – 15 November 2013 (study turbines) and the remainder were found at 37 turbines searched by Stantec from 1 April – 7 – June and by AESLM staff from 11 June 11 November. Fatality estimates for the 2013 monitoring period, based on the results at the 24 study turbines and taking into account search interval, carcass persistence, – – searcher efficiency, and an area correction factor, were 1.4 (95% CI 0.7 2.2) bats and 3.4 (95% CI 2.0 5.0) birds per turbine. ## **1.0 Introduction**

AES Laurel Mountain Wind, LLC (AESLM) began operation of the Laurel Mountain Wind Energy Project (Project) in Randolph and Barbour Counties, West Virginia in July 2011. Cut-in wind speeds of Project turbines have varied seasonally since the site became operational based on collaboration with the US Fish and Wildlife Service Elkins Field Office (USFWS) and WV Department of Natural Resources (WVDNR; Table 1). Stantec Consulting Services Inc. (Stantec) has conducted post-construction bird and bat fatality monitoring on a seasonal basis at the Project since mid-August 2011 (Table 1). Fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 monitoring involved comparison of three operational treatments: normally operating turbines (control turbines), turbines fully feathered below wind speeds of 3.5 meters per second (m/s), and turbines fully feathered below wind speeds of 4.5 m/s. During fall 2012 and spring, summer, and fall 2013, all turbines were operated according to a sliding scale based on acoustic bat activity recorded on 6 turbine nacelles during fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012. Under this system, turbine cutin speeds were (b) (4) and (b) (4) such that turbines were fully feathered during conditions when 99 percent of acoustic bat activity occurred at turbine height. This plan was implemented in early September through 15 November 2012, and again between 1 April and 15 November 2013 as approved by the USFWS in coordination with WVDNR.

A work scope for year 2013 monitoring was presented to the USFWS and WVDNR in mid-March 2013. On 28 March 2013, the USFWS requested that all 61 Project turbines be included in the standardized 3-day search interval rather than the 24 turbines surveyed in 2011 and 2012. In coordination with AESLM, Stantec mobilized additional staff to the site such that all turbines were monitored at a 3-day interval beginning 1 April 2013. In response to requests from AESLM, the USFWS agreed to reduce the level of standardized monitoring back to 24 turbines as of 7 June 2013 provided that AESLM operations staff conducted weekly monitoring at the remaining 37 turbines to document incidental carcasses. AESLM developed a protocol for operations staff to conduct weekly surveys at the 37 turbines not surveyed by Stantec and initiated these surveys on 11 June 2013. In coordination with USFWS, AES increased the number of turbines with nacelle-mounted acoustic detectors from 6 to 9 in mid-April, 2013. This report summarizes results of standardized post-construction surveys conducted at the Project between 1 April and 15 November 2013.

## **1.1 STUDY AREA AND PROJECT DESCRIPTION**

The Project is a 97.6-megawatt (MW) facility located on private property leased by the land owners to AESLM.  The Project occupies 13 kilometers (km) (8 miles) of the ridgeline of Laurel Mountain in northeastern West Virginia (Figure 1-1).  The Project is on the boundary between Randolph and Barbour Counties, near the town of Elkins, and consists of a linear ridgeline oriented northeast to southwest, with ridgetop elevations ranging from approximately 800 to 900 meters (m) (2,625 feet [’] to 2,953’).  The

western side of the ridgeline is more gradually sloped than the eastern side, which drops off steeply.  The minimum elevation in the valleys surrounding Laurel Mountain is approximately 545 m (1,788’), resulting in an elevation differential of approximately 255 to 355 m (837’ to 1,165’) be tween valley and ridgetop.  .

Construction of the facility occurred between spring 2010 and mid-summer 2011, with the sixty-one 1.6 MW GE XLE wind turbines becoming operational in July 2011.  Each turbine has a hub height of 80 m (262’) and a rotor diameter of 82.5 m (271’), resulting in a maximum blade tip height of approximately 122 m (400’) and a rotor swept area (RSA) of approximately 5,343 m[2] (57,512 ft[2] ).  Of the 61 turbines, 22 include a single synchronized flashing red light compliant with Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) standards.  Turbines normally operate at wind speeds between approximately 3.5 m/s (7.8 miles per hour [mph]) and 25.0 m/s (56 mph), and rotate at speeds between 10 and 18 revolutions per minute (RPM).

In addition to the 61 turbines, the Project includes a single gravel access road running the length of the project, an Operation and Maintenance (O&M) facility at the southern end of the Project, and two 80meter, guyed meteorological towers with flashing red lighting.  The Project also includes an electrical substation and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), both of which are located near the midpoint of the Project where an existing utility-owned transmission line, utility-owned electrical switchyard, and county road cross the ridgeline.

## **2.2 TURBINE SELECTION AND TRANSECT ESTABLISHMENT**

Based on feedback from the USFWS in late March 2013, Stantec initially searched all 61 Project turbines through early June 2013, after which the USFWS agreed to reduce the standardized survey effort to the 24 turbines monitored in 2011 and 2012 (see Figure 1-1). These 24 turbines are evenly distributed across the Project area including peaks and low areas, with prioritization given to turbines with large, relatively flat cleared areas with centered turbines to maximize the searchable area.

A grid of parallel linear transects up to 90 m (295’) on a side was established at each o f the searched turbines, with transects spaced at 5- m (16’) intervals, oriented north -south (magnetic) and centered on the turbine.  This plot size was chosen based on a combination of turbine clearing size (generally ~35 to 45 m radius from the turbine) and available literature suggesting that most bat carcasses fall within 30 m to 40 m of turbines (Kerns and Kerlinger 2004, Johnson et al. 2003, Young et al. 2011).  Transects on the east side of turbines were numbered 1E through 9E and transects on the west side of turbines were numbered 1W to 9W, with the lowest number nearest the turbine.  Transect grids were pre-loaded onto a Global Positioning System (GPS) unit (Trimble Geo-XH) and marked in the field around searched turbines using wooden stakes, fluorescent flagging tape, and/or fluorescent marking paint.  The boundary of the searchable area surrounding each turbine, defined by the point at which the transect grid ended or met either the edge of the cleared area around the turbine or slopes that were too steep or rugged to survey, was located using the same GPS used to establish transects.  The searchable area around each surveyed turbine was calculated and mapped using AutoCAD software.  Appendix A contains maps of the extent of searchable area, including numbered transects for each of the 24 turbines monitored throughout the 2013 survey period.

## **2.3 FATALITY SURVEY METHODS**

Post-construction surveys were conducted on 3-day intervals at each searched turbine.  Unless prevented by inclement weather severe enough to compromise the safety of the surveyors or other factors preventing safe access to turbines, surveys occurred at a subset of searched turbines 7 days per week. The order in which turbines were searched and the direction in which surveyors walked transects varied among days. Surveyors maintained a steady, slow walking pace of approximately 35 to 45 m per minute (115’ to 148’ per minute) along each marked transect, visually scanning the ground within 2 m to 3 m (7’ to 10’) of both sides of each transect. Although survey conditions changed between days based on weather, ground cover conditions and other factors, surveyors attempted to keep search times per turbine as consistent as possible among surveyors and survey days throughout the survey period.

When a carcass was found during a survey, it was marked with a highly visible temporary marker, so that it was easily located for post-survey processing. Surveyors completed searching that particular turbine, marking any additional carcasses in a similar manner. At the conclusion of the turbine search, surveyors returned to inspect and process each carcass and recorded the distance and azimuth from the turbine to the carcass using a digital rangefinder and magnetic compass. Carcasses were identified in the field when possible and collected in a sealed plastic bag, labeled with a given carcass’ unique identification number

and the information collected on site at the time that carcass was found. Surveyors recorded the date; time; turbine number; transect number; species, age, sex, and condition of carcass; distance and azimuth from turbine; general weather conditions such as cloud cover, precipitation and temperature; and any other notes regarding each carcass. Carcasses were stored in an off-site freezer owned by Stantec after the completion of daily surveys.

The general condition of each carcass was noted, including evidence of scavenging or presence of insects, to estimate freshness of the carcass. The amount of time since the fatality occurred was estimated based on the condition of the eyes and fur or feathers, the degree to which insect scavengers were present on the carcass, and the level of decomposition or desiccation. Carcasses were determined to be “fresh” if they had relatively intact plumage or pelage and little or no insect scavenging, such as removal of eyes. Visible signs of trauma such as broken wings or lacerations on a fresh carcass were also noted. Searchers took photos of each carcass. Carcasses determined to be Myotis species or identified as potential Myotis species were provided to biologists at the WVDNR for verification. Carcasses that were in too poor condition to be properly identified to species were classified as accurately as possible, or classified as “unknown”. Carcasses present at the beginning of the 2013 survey period that had obviously died prior to the survey periods were collected and identified, but were not included in estimates of total fatality.

Carcasses found by Stantec searchers outside the daily search periods, outside the turbine search plots, or found by project operations staff and reported to Stantec, were considered incidental finds and were collected, identified, and stored according to the same protocols described above. Incidental carcasses found within surveyed areas at the 24 searched turbines (during times when surveyors were on site for other purposes or reported by AESLM personnel) were included in estimates of overall fatality as if they had been found during the next scheduled search, following the methods of Young et al. (2011) used at Mount Storm. Incidental carcasses found outside surveyed areas or at non-searched turbines were not used in calculating overall estimated fatality rates. Similarly, carcasses found by Stantec at the 37 additional turbines searched only between 1 April and 7 June 2013 or by AESLM personnel after 7 June 2013 were considered incidental and not included in estimated fatality rates.

## **2.3.1 Searcher Efficiency Trials**

Searcher efficiency trials were conducted throughout the survey period to quantify the ability of searchers to detect carcasses within the survey plots. Trial carcasses were placed at representative locations within search plots such that the searcher being tested was unaware that a trial was taking place. Searchers were unaware of the date and time of trials, and trial blindness was further ensured by varying the number of carcasses placed and the number of turbines with trial carcasses. Although trial carcasses were discreetly marked using a small piece of string tied around a leg to identify them as trial carcasses, searchers did not inspect the carcasses until the end of a turbine search. Searchers were therefore unaware that a trial had taken place until their turbine search was complete.

Searcher efficiency trials were conducted throughout the monitoring period, subject to carcass availability, with trials conducted in a variety of weather conditions. Trial coordinators would predetermine the turbines at which carcasses would be placed and would select trial locations that were representative of cover types in the search area. Carcasses were placed to ensure that the strings marking

them as trials were only visible when the carcasses were picked up. Trial carcasses consisted of birds and bats found at Laurel Mountain, so composition of carcasses in terms of carcass size and ratio of birds or bats relied upon availability of carcasses found at the site. While most trial carcasses had been previously frozen, we selected carcasses in reasonably good condition for use in searcher efficiency trials. Trial carcasses were removed following each trial to prevent the loss of carcasses to scavengers, prevent potential attraction to the site by scavengers, and so that they would be available for use in subsequent trials.

Searcher efficiency (p) was expressed as the proportion of trial carcasses found by searchers: the number of trial carcasses successfully found by searchers divided by the total number of trial carcasses available during searcher efficiency trials. Trial carcasses removed by scavengers before the turbine was surveyed were considered invalid and were removed from the dataset. Trial carcasses that were found by the surveyor being tested were considered successful trials, and collected by that surveyor. Trial carcasses that were not found by the surveyor being tested were considered unsuccessful trials and were recovered by the trial coordinator, such that a surveyor had only one opportunity to find a trial carcass.

## **2.3.2 Carcass Removal Trials**

Carcass removal trials were conducted periodically throughout the survey period to quantify the length of time before carcasses were removed as well as to record qualitative information on the rate at which carcasses decomposed, dried, or were consumed by insects. During each trial, a carcass was placed in a known location at a given turbine, marked discreetly using a small piece of string, and monitored daily for the subsequent 14 days. Trials were placed at multiple turbines during the same trial period to provide a range of sampled locations and conditions. Carcasses were removed at the conclusion of the trial if still present. Observers recorded the date on which the carcass was entirely removed by scavengers or at which point the carcasses had decomposed or degraded beyond recognition.

Stantec conducted carcass removal trials throughout the monitoring period based on availability of carcasses, and made an effort to ensure that carcasses used in trials were of similar, relatively fresh condition, and had been handled minimally. Carcasses used during trials were birds and bats found during fatality surveys at Laurel Mountain, so carcass composition was dependent on fatality patterns at the site. While most carcasses used in trials had been previously frozen, we selected carcasses in as fresh condition as possible for carcass removal trials. Trial carcasses were placed at each searched turbine and in a variety of cover types and distances from turbines so that the combined trial dataset was representative of the variety of turbine locations and ground cover types present in the project area. Carcasses that were not present on the day following placement were considered to have been scavenged on day 1 of the trial and so on up to the 14th day of the trial, when carcasses that were still present were recovered.

Carcass persistence was calculated using a maximum likelihood estimator as employed by Erickson et al. (2003) and Good et al. (2011).  Due to an uneven ratio of bat versus bird carcasses available in 2011, carcass removal data from fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 were combined to generate overall estimates of carcass persistence for birds and bats. ## **2.4 DATA ANALYSIS AND ESTIMATED FATALITY RATES**

Estimates of total bird and bat fatality rates, adjusted for carcass removal rates, searcher efficiency, and area searched, followed the widely used method developed by Erikson et al. (2003), incorporating the Shoenfeld estimator for bias adjustment, as was done for fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 surveys (Shoenfeld 2004). The same methods were used by Young et al. (2011) to calculate fatality estimates for surveys conducted at the NedPower Mount Storm Wind Energy Facility in northeastern West Virginia. Total estimated fatality was calculated separately for birds and bats within each operational treatment, and reported as a total number of mortalities per turbine per survey period. Fatality estimates were also reported per megawatt (MW) and per 1000 m[2] of rotor swept area (RSA). Estimated fatality rates were calculated for birds and for bats in the fall 2011 period, the spring/summer 2012 period, and the combined survey period.

Searcher efficiency and scavenger removal trials were combined to derive a season-specific fatality adjustment ( _π_ ), using the following formula, where _I_ (the search interval) = 3, _p_ = the overall proportion of carcasses recovered in searcher efficiency trials, and _t_ = the mean number of days carcasses remained in the study area, as calculated above. This value represents the likelihood that a carcass would ultimately be found by searchers after multiple survey days, combining search interval, searcher efficiency, and carcass persistence rates. This value was calculated separately for birds and bats based on the results of searcher efficiency and scavenger removal trials for each group. Estimates of searcher efficiency and carcass persistence for birds and bats were assumed to be the same among turbines in different operational treatments.

Fatality estimates were adjusted to account for area searched versus potential search area, and distribution of carcasses around turbines. A multiplier, _A_ , was calculated based on the percentage of area

searched within seven 10 m bands surrounding each turbine, searcher efficiency, and numbers of carcasses found within each 10 m band. _A_ was calculated separately for birds and bats according to the following formula, as described in Young et al. (2011), where _ck_ equals the number of carcasses within the k[th] distance band, _p_ equals searcher efficiency, and _sk_ equals the proportion of area searched within the k[th] distance band across searched turbines.

Total fatality ( _m_ ), representing the number of mortalities estimated per turbine for the corresponding survey period, was then estimated separately for birds and bats using the following equation, where _c_ = the mean number of fatalities documented per turbine, _A_ = the area correction, and _π_ adjusts for searcher efficiency and scavenger removal rates. Incidental carcasses found at the 24 searched turbines outside normal survey times were included in fatality estimates although other incidental carcasses were excluded.

Bootstrapping methods were used to determine 95 percent confidence intervals (95% CI) surrounding each estimate, which were established using quantiles of the bootstrapped samples (Erickson et al. 2003, Young et al. 2011). CI for searcher efficiency were calculated by choosing 5,000 random samples (with replacement) from the trial data set and calculating a searcher efficiency rate for each sample. CI for carcass persistence rates were calculated by choosing 5,000 random samples (with replacement) from the trial data set and calculating a carcass persistence rate for each sample. An additional 5,000 samples of observed fatality were derived by choosing a random set of turbines 5,000 times and summing the total number of carcasses found at each turbine in the sample. The fatality adjustment ( _π_ ) and total fatality ( _m_ were calculated for each bootstrapped sample.

## **3.2.2 Species Composition**

Including all carcasses found at the 24 study turbines and 37 additional turbines in 2013, 22 bat and 42 bird carcasses were collected at Laurel Mountain. Four bat species were documented including silverhaired bat, hoary bat, eastern red bat, and big brown bat (Table 3-3). Long-distance migratory species accounted for 95% of bat carcasses found in 2013. No _Myotis_ species or unknown bats were collected. Of the 22 total bat carcasses, 11 (50%) were male, 5 (23%) were female, and 6 (27%) were of an unknown sex. Twelve bird species were documented including red-eyed vireo, wood duck, golden-crowned kinglet, redwinged blackbird, yellow-rumped warbler and turkey vulture (Table 3-4). No threatened or endangered bird or bat species were found during 2013 surveys.

## **3.2.3 Searcher Efficiency Trials**

Stantec placed 89 bat and 129 bird carcasses for a total of 218 attempted searcher efficiency trials during the 2013 monitoring period. Of these, 5 bat and 8 bird carcasses were removed by scavengers during the trial period and were removed from the dataset resulting in 84 valid bat and 121 valid bird searcher efficiency trials. Trials were placed on 18 separate occasions between early May and early November. Searchers recovered 52 bat trial carcasses (62%) and 57 bird trial carcasses (47%) during the 2013 monitoring period.

Trial carcasses were placed at 40 different turbines and consisted of birds and bats found previously at the site. As such, trial carcasses were considered representative of the types and sizes of carcasses typically found at the Project. Due to the small number of medium and large bird carcasses found on site, we were not able to estimate searcher efficiency rates according to carcass size. Trial carcasses were placed in a variety of ground cover conditions, and at variable distances and azimuths from turbines to accurately represent the range of ground cover types and conditions present at searched turbines.

## **4.0 Discussion**

## **4.1 TURBINE OPERATION**

The customized cut-in wind speed curtailment system appeared to perform as designed throughout the 2013 monitoring period. Comparison of turbine RPM during particular combinations of (b) (4) and wind speed during the day and at night reveals for the 24 study turbines indicated that turbines were remaining curtailed during the conditions specified in the sliding scale developed for the site in cooperation with the USFWS and WVDNR. No faults of the system were reported by AES during the monitoring period.

## **4.2 BAT AND BIRD FATALITY PATTERNS**

Typically, most bat mortalities occur during late summer and early fall, coinciding with autumn migration (Arnett and Baerwald 2013, Arnett 2008). During the 2013 monitoring period at Laurel Mountain, no bat carcasses were found between 14 July and 15 September, and only 2 (9%) bat carcasses were found during June, July, and August combined. This unusual seasonal pattern in bat fatality is therefore likely attributable to the customized proprietary curtailment system, which was designed to be most restrictive at times of highest bat activity. Because the system implemented (b) (4)

(b) (4) , turbines were curtailed for a larger percent of the night and at higher wind speeds in July and August and lesser amounts of time during May and October, when 68% of the 22 bat carcasses documented at the 24 study turbines were found.

More bird carcasses were found at the 24 study turbines during November than any other month in 2013. Although bird carcasses were found during all months in the study period, no more than 12 carcasses were found during a single month, including incidentals and results from searches of all 61 turbines that occurred between 1 April and 7 June (fully encompassing the spring songbird migration period).

Species composition of bat fatality was consistent with results of previous monitoring at the site and similar studies in the region, with long-distance migratory species accounting for most bat fatality. Species composition of bird fatality was consistent with similar studies in that songbirds accounted for most bird carcasses found. The discovery of 5 wood ducks (12% of bird carcasses found in 2013) between 3 and 5 November appeared to have coincided with a migration event, based on the lack of suitable wood duck habitat in proximity to the site. Raptor carcasses found in 2013 included 3 turkey vultures, 2 redtailed hawks, and one unknown hawk. Carcass searchers noted increased red-tailed hawk activity on site throughout the 2013 monitoring period relative to previous years at the site.

Spatial distribution of carcasses in 2013 was similar to that documented in previous survey periods. Carcass persistence was slightly less in 2013 relative to the fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 survey – period, when carcasses persistence was estimated to be 6.6 days (95% CI 5.2 8.4) for bats and 7.1 days – (95% CI 5.2 9.7) for birds. Sample sizes of carcass persistence trials were adequate during both monitoring periods, so the reduced estimate of carcass persistence could be the result of slightly increased scavenger activity at the site. Stantec surveyors noted high levels of American crow activity on site throughout the monitoring period, and made an anecdotal observation of crows removing a trial carcass. Other potential scavengers include a variety of wildlife species present on site.

Searcher efficiency estimates during the 2013 monitoring period were similar to those from the fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 monitoring period, with searcher efficiency slightly higher for bats than birds. Periodic mowing of vegetation at the study turbines by AESLM improved visibility of the ground.

## **4.3 COMPARISON TO PREVIOUS SURVEYS**

The 2013 monitoring period at Laurel Mountain was the fourth distinct monitoring period at the site, and the first to span the entire period from 1 April through 15 November during a single calendar year without interruption or a change in turbine operational curtailment. Therefore, although previous data from the site exist for comparison, no two monitoring periods represent the same operational conditions and same seasonal time period. Monitoring during fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 enabled comparison of three operational scenarios, each with 8 turbines. During the fall 2012 and year 2013 monitoring periods, all searched turbines were operated under the same operational scheme designed to avoid potential impacts to listed bat species. Bat fatality estimates have differed substantially among monitoring periods at Laurel Mountain, due primarily to the variable curtailment parameters used in Fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 versus fall 2012 and year 2013. The bat fatality estimate most representative of fully operational turbines was 23.4 bats/turbine derived from the control turbines in the combined fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 monitoring period (6.5 months of monitoring). The estimate of 1.4 bats/turbine for the 2013 monitoring period was 94% less than the 2011/2012 control estimate, and included the full 7.5 months between 1 April and 15 November.   For comparison purposes only, assuming the level of bat mortality observed at control turbines in the second half of August 2011 at Laurel Mountain remained consistent throughout all of August 2011 the level of bat mortality at control turbines at Laurel Mountain would have been approximately 32.8 bats/turbine for a simulated 7.5 month study period.  Were the 2011/2012 and 2013 monitoring periods both able to include the same 7.5 months of monitoring, the cut-in speed curtailment strategy employed in 2013 would therefore have reduced bat mortality by an estimated 96%  in comparison to 2011/2012 control turbines.

Bird fatality estimate confidence intervals for 2013 were relatively narrow, indicating fairly consistent carcass counts among the searched turbines.  No pattern of significantly higher bird mortality was observed at any of the turbines.

## **4.4 CURTAILMENT EVALUATION**

Based on the low bat fatality estimates derived in fall 2012 and year 2013, the customized sliding scale curtailment system appears highly effective at reducing risk of bat fatality at Laurel Mountain. The bat fatality estimate was 94% less than estimated from fully operational turbines at the site based on a shorter monitoring period, and is estimated to be approximately 96% lower when normalized for equivalent monitoring periods.  The number of bat carcasses found per turbine was generally consistent among monitored turbines, indicating little inter-turbine variability in effectiveness of the system. As no turbines at Laurel Mountain were fully operational during 2013, the “control” estimates derived from the combined fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 period provide the best data for comparison. The curtailment system was reliable and AES noted no failures of the automated system at any turbine – throughout the 1 April 15 November 2013 study period.

The USFWS established a goal of reducing overall bat fatality rates by 95% relative to the estimate for control turbines at this site as a way to demonstrate reduced risk of protected species fatalities, and the system appears to have met this goal.
